questions.question: How do you identify classes from a problem statement in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to extract entities from requirements and map them to object-oriented design elements — the foundational skill of Low-Level Design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every noun as a class without filtering, or missing behavioral entities like managers and controllers.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you'd also identify relationships (has-a, is-a) and potential design patterns while reading the problem statement.

questions.direct_answer: Identify nouns in the problem statement — these become candidate classes. Filter to entities that have both data (attributes) and behavior (methods). Actors become interfaces or abstract classes.

items: Nouns → candidate classes: Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, Payment
Verbs → methods on classes: park(), calculateFee(), issueTicket()
Not everything needs its own class: simple value objects can be fields
Actors (users, systems): often interfaces or abstract classes
Value objects vs entities: ParkingSpot (entity) vs Price (value object)
Group related attributes together into a class

answer_sections.content: My technique for identifying classes: I underline all the nouns in the problem statement. For a parking lot: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, car, motorcycle, ticket, payment, display board. These are my candidate classes. Then I filter: does it have meaningful attributes AND behaviors? ParkingSpot has attributes (spotId, type, isOccupied) and behaviors (occupy(), free(), isAvailable()) — it's a class. 'Price' might just be a BigDecimal field, not its own class. Verbs tell me what methods belong to which class: 'issue a ticket' → Ticket has an issueTicket() or the ParkingLot has issueTicket() that creates a Ticket. I also identify abstract concepts: Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle.

Simple values like price may just be a field — not every noun needs its own class

candidates miss: identifying abstract concepts. Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle — make that explicit early or you'll redesign later.

speakable_v2.cap: Underline nouns, filter by attributes-plus-behaviors, then check for abstract concepts. That three-step scan will get you a solid class list in two minutes.

sections.title: Extracting Classes from Requirements
sections.content: Class identification is the first step in translating a problem statement into object-oriented design. The process starts by **underlining all nouns** in the requirements — these are your candidate entities. A parking lot problem mentions "vehicle, spot, ticket, floor, payment" — each is a potential class. But not every noun becomes a class: filter for entities that have **both state and behavior**. "Vehicle" has attributes (license plate, type) and behavior (can park, can exit). "Spot" has state (occupied/free) and behavior (reserve, release). Pure data containers without logic might become **value objects** or records instead of full classes. **Actors** in the system (Admin, Customer, Attendant) often become interfaces or abstract classes if multiple implementations exist. The key insight: classes represent concepts that have **identity, lifecycle, and responsibilities** in your domain.

sections.title: Identifying Classes from a Parking Lot Problem
Key Points
content: **Noun extraction**: Circle all nouns in the problem statement — they're your starting point for entities.
**Behavior filter**: Keep only entities that have both attributes and methods; pure data becomes records or value objects.
**Actor mapping**: Users, admins, and operators often become interfaces (Parkable, Payable) or abstract classes (User).
**Relationship identification**: Look for has-a (ParkingLot has Floors), is-a (Car is-a Vehicle), and uses (Ticket uses Vehicle).
**Avoid primitive obsession**: If a noun like "spot ID" appears repeatedly with validation logic, make it a class (SpotId).
**Manager classes**: Verbs like "calculate fee" or "generate ticket" hint at service classes (FeeCalculator, TicketGenerator).
**Domain language**: Use exact business terms — if the problem says "bay" instead of "spot", your class should be ParkingBay.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd start by reading the problem statement carefully and underlining all the nouns — those are my candidate classes. For a parking lot system, I'd see vehicle, spot, floor, ticket, payment, entry panel. Then I'd filter: does this noun have both data and behavior? Vehicle has a license plate and type, and it can enter or exit. That's a class. Spot has availability status and can be reserved or freed. That's a class too. But something like "spot number" is just a string attribute, not a class. Next, I'd look at the actors. If there's a customer and an attendant, I might make a User interface or abstract class if they share behavior. Verbs in the problem also matter. If it says "calculate parking fee", that's a hint I need a FeeCalculator service class. One mistake freshers make is creating a class for every single noun without thinking about responsibility. You don't need a class for "color" if it's just a String field. The goal is to model entities that have identity and a clear job in the system. I'd also sketch the relationships while reading — ParkingLot has-a list of Floors, Floor has-a list of Spots. That helps me see the structure before I write any code.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when to use inheritance versus interface contracts in object-oriented design — a core LLD decision point.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using abstract classes everywhere or not knowing Java 8+ allows default methods in interfaces, blurring the distinction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java allows multiple interfaces but only single inheritance, so interfaces are preferred for flexibility.

questions.direct_answer: Abstract class provides partial implementation with fields and concrete methods for IS-A relationships with shared code (Vehicle with common fields). Interface is a pure contract with no state for CAN-DO relationships (Payable, Parkable). Use interface for type hierarchy, abstract class for shared implementation.

answer_sections.content: In LLD, I use abstract class when there's a clear IS-A relationship with shared implementation. Vehicle is abstract because all vehicles share common attributes (licensePlate, size, color) and the subclasses (Car, Motorcycle) build on that. I use interfaces for capabilities or contracts that can apply to unrelated classes. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A but both can be paid for. The rule: abstract class for shared code in a family of classes; interface for defining a contract that any class can implement. In modern Java, interfaces can have default methods, which blurs this a bit, but the design intent remains distinct.

follow_up_questions: Can a class extend an abstract class and implement interfaces simultaneously?
When would you change a class to an interface in a design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Abstract class vs interface is one of the most common LLD follow-ups — and the answer isn't about Java syntax, it's about design intent.

groups.heading: Abstract Class
groups.text: A partial implementation meant to be extended. Use it when related classes share code. Vehicle is abstract because Car and Motorcycle both need licensePlate, color, and size fields.

groups.heading: Interface
groups.text: A contract that defines capabilities. Use it when unrelated classes need the same behavior. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A, but both can be paid for.

beats.text: Use abstract class for shared code in a family. Use interface for defining a capability that any class can implement. When in doubt, start with an interface — it's easier to loosen later than to break inheritance hierarchies.
sharp edge: Java interfaces now support default methods, which blurs the line. But the design intent still matters — don't use default methods to smuggle shared state into an interface.

speakable_v2.cap: Abstract class = shared code for an IS-A family. Interface = a contract for a CAN-DO capability. Start with interface when you're unsure.
followup_handoff: Can a class extend an abstract class and implement interfaces at the same time?
When would you refactor a class to an interface?

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface in Design Decisions
sections.content: The choice between **abstract class** and **interface** hinges on whether you're modeling shared implementation or a behavioral contract. An **abstract class** is for IS-A relationships where subclasses share common fields and methods. In a parking lot, Vehicle is abstract with fields like licensePlate and a concrete method getType() — Car and Motorcycle inherit this shared code. An **interface** is for CAN-DO capabilities that unrelated classes can implement. Payable is an interface implemented by Ticket, Subscription, and Fine — they're not related by inheritance, just by the ability to be paid. Java 8+ complicates this: interfaces can now have default methods with implementation, but they still can't hold instance state (fields). The practical rule: use interfaces for type contracts and multiple capability modeling, use abstract classes when you have shared state or implementation that subclasses shouldn't redefine.

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content: Use an **abstract class** when subclasses share fields and non-trivial implementation. In an ATM system, Account is abstract with fields like accountNumber and balance, and a concrete method getBalance(). SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount inherit this state. You can't achieve this with an interface because interfaces can't hold instance variables. Use an **interface** when you want to define a capability that unrelated classes can implement. Payable is implemented by Ticket, Fine, and Subscription — they're not part of the same inheritance tree, but they all support payment. Interfaces also let you model multiple contracts: a class can be both Parkable and Payable. Since Java allows multiple interfaces but only one parent class, interfaces give you design flexibility. If you're designing a new feature and unsure, start with an interface — it's less committal than locking into a class hierarchy.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Inheritance limit**: Java allows one abstract parent but many interfaces — design for flexibility with interfaces.
**State vs contract**: Abstract classes carry shared state (fields); interfaces define behavior contracts (methods).
**IS-A vs CAN-DO**: Abstract class for "Car is-a Vehicle"; interface for "Ticket can-do Payable".
**Default methods**: Java 8+ interfaces can have default implementations, but still can't hold instance state.
**Refactoring safety**: Changing an abstract class affects all subclasses; adding a default method to an interface is backward-compatible.
**LLD naming**: Abstract classes often end in base domain nouns (Vehicle, Account); interfaces end in -able or describe actions (Payable, Searchable).
**Multiple capabilities**: Use interfaces when a class needs multiple roles — PremiumSpot implements Parkable and Reservable.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is about shared implementation versus contract definition. An abstract class is for when you have a family of related classes that share common fields and behavior. In a parking lot design, I'd make Vehicle an abstract class with a license plate field and a method to check if it fits in a spot. Then Car and Motorcycle extend Vehicle and inherit that code. You use abstract class for IS-A relationships where there's real shared state. An interface is different — it's a pure contract that says what a class can do, without sharing any implementation. I'd make Payable an interface with a method like processPayment. Then Ticket, Subscription, and Fine all implement Payable, even though they're completely different entities. They just share the ability to be paid. The key thing is Java only allows single inheritance, so you can extend one abstract class but implement many interfaces. That's why interfaces are more flexible. If I'm designing a new feature, I usually start with an interface unless I know for sure I have shared state to inherit. One gotcha: since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods with code, but they still can't hold instance fields like an abstract class can. So if you need shared fields, you need an abstract class.

questions.question: How do you define the responsibilities of each class in an LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to apply the Single Responsibility Principle in practice — assigning clear, focused responsibilities to each class.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating god classes that do everything (ParkingLot handles spots, fees, tickets, users) or splitting too granularly.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you'd validate responsibilities by asking 'what would cause this class to change?' — if multiple answers, split it.

questions.direct_answer: Apply SRP: each class should have one reason to change. ParkingSpot manages spot availability. FeeCalculator calculates fees. TicketGenerator creates tickets. Don't combine unrelated behaviors in one class.

answer_sections.content: I apply the Single Responsibility Principle: each class should have one primary reason to change. In a parking lot: ParkingSpot's job is tracking whether it's occupied and what type it is — nothing about pricing. FeeCalculator calculates fees based on time and vehicle type — nothing about spots. TicketGenerator creates and manages tickets. ParkingLot coordinates the overall flow: find a spot, issue a ticket, process exit. A sign of poor SRP is a 'God class' that knows about spots, fees, tickets, and display boards. When you ask 'why would this class change?' and get three different answers, it needs to be split. Each business rule change should ideally only require changing one class.

follow_up_questions: How does SRP relate to the concept of cohesion?
What happens to your design if you violate SRP?

beats.text: SRP says each class should have one primary reason to change. It's the most practical LLD principle because it directly shapes which classes you create and what goes in each.

groups.heading: FeeCalculator

speakable_v2.cap: Give each class one job. If you can describe a class's responsibility in one short sentence, you're on the right track.

sections.title: Assigning Responsibilities Using SRP
sections.content: Defining class responsibilities is about applying the **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)**: each class should have one reason to change. In a parking lot, don't make ParkingLot responsible for spot allocation, fee calculation, and ticket generation — those are three different concerns that change for different reasons. **ParkingSpot** has one job: manage its own availability (reserve, release, check status). **FeeCalculator** has one job: compute parking fees based on duration and vehicle type. **TicketGenerator** creates and validates tickets. The test: ask "why would this class change?" If the answer is "when fee rules change" AND "when spot types change", you've violated SRP. In LLD interviews, responsibilities map to **domain verbs**: "calculate fee" becomes FeeCalculator.calculateFee(), "find spot" becomes SpotFinder.findAvailableSpot(). Avoid **god classes** that do everything and **anemic models** that do nothing (just getters/setters). Each class should have clear, cohesive behavior.

sections.title: Separating Responsibilities into Focused Classes
Key Points
content: **SRP test**: Ask "what would cause this class to change?" — if there are multiple unrelated answers, split the class.
**Domain verbs**: Responsibilities come from action words in requirements — "calculate" becomes a Calculator class.
**Avoid god classes**: Don't put spot management, fee calculation, and user authentication in one ParkingLot class.
**Avoid anemic models**: Don't make classes with only getters and setters — push behavior into the entity that owns the data.
**Manager pattern**: Use service classes (FeeCalculator, TicketGenerator) for operations that don't belong to a single entity.
**Change isolation**: If fee rules change, only FeeCalculator changes — spot logic and ticket generation stay untouched.
**Cohesion over coupling**: Methods in a class should operate on the same data; if they don't, they belong in different classes.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I define responsibilities by applying the Single Responsibility Principle — each class should have one clear reason to change. For a parking lot, I wouldn't make ParkingLot do everything. Instead, I'd split it up. ParkingSpot has one job: manage whether it's occupied or free. It has methods like reserve and release, and it knows its own state. FeeCalculator is separate — its only job is to take a ticket and calculate the parking fee based on duration and vehicle type. If the fee rules change, only FeeCalculator changes. TicketGenerator creates tickets. If we change ticket format or add a QR code, only that class changes. The way I validate this is by asking, what would cause this class to change? If the answer is multiple unrelated things like fee rules, spot types, and user authentication, I've created a god class and I need to split it. The mistake freshers make is either putting everything in one class or going too far the other way and creating a class for every single field. The balance is that each class should represent one concept or one operation. In practice, I look at the verbs in the requirements. If it says calculate fee, that's a hint I need a FeeCalculator. If it says find available spot, that's a SpotFinder or a method on ParkingFloor. Responsibilities should match the language of the problem domain.

questions.question: What are enums useful for in LLD and how do you use them?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of Java enums and their role in modeling domain-specific constants in Low-Level Design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using String constants or integers instead of enums, missing the type safety and behavior encapsulation enums provide.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that enums can have fields, constructors, and methods — they're not just constant lists but full classes.

questions.direct_answer: Enums represent fixed sets of constants with associated behavior. In LLD: VehicleType (CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK), SpotType (COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED), TicketStatus (ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED). Better than String constants.

answer_sections.content: Enums are extremely useful in LLD for representing a fixed set of states or types. Instead of using String constants or magic integers, enums give type safety and readability. In a parking lot: VehicleType enum with CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — now the compiler catches if I accidentally pass 'BUS' which isn't a valid type. SpotType with COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED. TicketStatus with ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED. Java enums can also carry data and behavior — SpotType.COMPACT can have a size field. Using enums in switch statements is clean and the compiler warns if you miss a case. They also make persistence more explicit — store the enum name as a string in the database.

follow_up_questions: How do you store an enum value in a database with JPA?
Can Java enums have abstract methods?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Enums are small but powerful — and every LLD that has types or states should be using them.

beats.text: Enums represent a fixed set of constants. In LLD they replace error-prone String constants and magic integers — and the compiler enforces valid values for you.

items: VehicleType: CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — type-safe vehicle classification
SpotType: COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED — each can carry a size field
TicketStatus: ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED — state machine for a ticket's lifecycle
PaymentMode: CASH, CARD, UPI — clean switch statements with compiler warnings if you miss a case

beats.text: SpotType.COMPACT can carry its own size field and a getSize() method. That's richer than a plain constant — it bundles the data and behavior that belong together.
non-obvious: Java enums can have abstract methods, meaning each constant can override the behavior differently. It's rarely needed in LLD interviews, but it shows depth if you mention it.

speakable_v2.cap: Reach for enums whenever you have a fixed set of types or states. They make your design safer, clearer, and easier to extend.

sections.title: Using Enums to Model Domain Constants
sections.content: Enums in Java are **type-safe constants with behavior**, far more powerful than strings or integers. In LLD, enums model **fixed sets of options** that don't change at runtime: VehicleType (CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK), SpotType (COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED), TicketStatus (ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED). Using enums instead of "car" strings prevents typos and makes your design self-documenting. Java enums are full classes: they can have **fields, constructors, and methods**. You can add a spotCount field to VehicleType and a method like requiresLargeSpot(). This encapsulates business rules directly in the constant. Enums also work seamlessly with switch statements and provide compile-time safety — if you add a new VehicleType, the compiler forces you to handle it everywhere. In LLD interviews, enums are a signal of **clean design**: they replace magic strings, centralize domain constants, and make your code easier to extend.

sections.title: Enums with Fields and Behavior in a Parking Lot
Key Points
content: **Type safety**: Enums prevent typos and invalid values — you can't pass "carr" instead of VehicleType.CAR.
**Behavior encapsulation**: Enums can have fields, constructors, and methods — they're not just constant lists.
**Domain modeling**: Use enums for fixed sets that don't change at runtime — vehicle types, spot types, payment methods, statuses.
**Switch exhaustiveness**: Java switch on enums can warn if you miss a case, making refactoring safer.
**Avoid magic strings**: Replace "active", "paid" strings with TicketStatus.ACTIVE, TicketStatus.PAID for clarity.
**Singleton guarantee**: Each enum constant is a singleton — there's exactly one instance of VehicleType.CAR.
**Business rules**: Put validation and calculation logic in enums — VehicleType.canFitIn(SpotType) keeps logic centralized.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Enums are super useful in LLD because they let you model fixed sets of constants in a type-safe way. Instead of using strings like "car" or "motorcycle", I'd create a VehicleType enum with CAR, MOTORCYCLE, and TRUCK as constants. That way, the compiler catches typos and I can't accidentally pass an invalid value. The cool thing about Java enums is they're not just lists of constants — they're full classes. I can add fields and methods to them. For example, I'd give VehicleType a spotsRequired field so MOTORCYCLE is one, CAR is two, and TRUCK is four. I can also add a method like calculateFee that returns the hourly rate for that vehicle type. That way, all the business logic related to vehicle types lives in one place. In a parking lot system, I'd use enums for things that have a fixed set of options: VehicleType, SpotType like COMPACT or LARGE, TicketStatus like ACTIVE or PAID, PaymentMethod like CASH or CARD. The mistake freshers make is using strings or integers for these — that's error-prone and you lose type safety. Enums also work great with switch statements. If I add a new vehicle type, the compiler will warn me everywhere I need to handle it. That makes the code much easier to maintain as requirements change.

questions.question: How do you model a one-to-many relationship in LLD Java classes?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of composition relationships and how to represent them in code using collections.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not encapsulating the collection properly — exposing the raw List directly instead of providing controlled access methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention defensive copying or returning unmodifiable collections to prevent external modification of internal state.

questions.direct_answer: Use a collection field: ParkingLot has List<ParkingFloor> floors. The 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many' side. Add methods to add, remove, and query from the collection.

answer_sections.content: One-to-many in Java classes is straightforward: the 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. ParkingLot has a List<ParkingFloor>. ParkingFloor has a Map<String, ParkingSpot> keyed by spot ID. The choice of collection type matters: List for ordered sequences, Set for unique items, Map for keyed lookup. I expose the relationship through methods rather than directly exposing the collection: addFloor(), getAvailableSpots(vehicleType), rather than getFloors() which exposes the internal list. This encapsulation lets me change the internal structure later — switch from List to Map for better spot lookup performance — without changing callers.

follow_up_questions: When would you use a Map instead of a List for a one-to-many relationship?
How do you handle bidirectional relationships in LLD?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: One-to-many is the most common relationship in LLD — and Java collections are exactly how you express it.

beats.text: A one-to-many relationship means one object owns or contains multiple instances of another. In Java, the 'one' side holds a collection field pointing to the 'many' side.

ParkingLot has a List of ParkingFloor. Each ParkingFloor has a Map keyed by spotId to ParkingSpot. The Map is better than a List here because you'll look up a spot by ID far more often than you'll iterate in order.

items: List: use when order matters or you need index access
Set: use when uniqueness matters and order doesn't
Map: use when you need fast lookup by a key — spot ID, vehicle license plate

beats.text: gotcha: don't expose the internal collection directly via a getFloors() getter. Expose it through meaningful methods like addFloor() and findAvailableSpot(). This lets you change the internal data structure later without breaking callers.

speakable_v2.cap: The 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. Choose List, Set, or Map based on how you'll query — and encapsulate the collection behind meaningful methods.

sections.title: Modeling One-to-Many Relationships
sections.content: A **one-to-many relationship** represents ownership or composition: one entity contains multiple instances of another. In a parking lot, ParkingLot has many ParkingFloors, and each ParkingFloor has many ParkingSpots. In Java, model this by holding a **collection field** (List, Set, Map) in the 'one' side. The 'one' entity is responsible for managing the lifecycle of the 'many' entities. ParkingLot creates, adds, and removes floors; it doesn't just reference them. Use **encapsulation**: don't expose the raw List<ParkingFloor> with a getter — provide controlled access methods like addFloor(), getFloor(int index), or getAllFloors() that returns an unmodifiable view. This prevents external code from corrupting your internal state. In LLD, one-to-many shows up everywhere: Order has many OrderItems, Account has many Transactions, ParkingFloor has many Spots. The collection type matters: **List** for ordered, **Set** for uniqueness, **Map** for key-based lookup. Choose based on how you'll access the 'many' side.

sections.title: One-to-Many Relationship Between ParkingLot and Floors
Key Points
content: **Collection field**: The 'one' side holds a List, Set, or Map of the 'many' side — ParkingLot has List<ParkingFloor> floors.
**Encapsulation**: Don't return the raw collection — use List.copyOf() or Collections.unmodifiableList() to protect internal state.
**Lifecycle ownership**: The 'one' side is responsible for creating, adding, and removing elements from the 'many' side.
**Access methods**: Provide addFloor(), removeFloor(), getFloor(id) instead of exposing the raw list with getFloors() that returns mutable state.
**Collection choice**: Use List for ordered access, Set for uniqueness, Map<K,V> for key-based lookup (e.g., Map<String, ParkingSpot> by spotId).
**Bidirectional caution**: If ParkingFloor also references ParkingLot, be careful of circular dependencies and memory leaks.
**Initialization**: Always initialize collections in the constructor (new ArrayList<>()) to avoid NullPointerException.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To model a one-to-many relationship, I'd use a collection field in the class on the 'one' side. For a parking lot system, ParkingLot has many ParkingFloors, so I'd add a private List of ParkingFloor inside ParkingLot. I'd initialize that list in the constructor so it's never null. Then I'd add methods to manage the collection, like addFloor to add a new floor, or findAvailableSpot that searches across all floors. The important thing is to not expose the raw list directly. If I have a getFloors method that returns the internal list, external code can add or remove floors without going through my controlled methods. That breaks encapsulation. Instead, I'd return an unmodifiable view using List.copyOf or Collections.unmodifiableList. That way, callers can see the floors but can't modify the internal state. I'd use the same pattern for ParkingFloor having many ParkingSpots — it holds a List of spots and provides methods like findSpotForVehicle. The collection type matters too. If order matters, I use a List. If I need fast lookup by ID, I'd use a Map with spot ID as the key. If I need to ensure no duplicates, I'd use a Set. One mistake freshers make is forgetting to initialize the collection, so they get a NullPointerException when they try to add something. Always initialize it in the constructor.
